title: GraphRAG and Knowledge Graphs
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# GraphRAG and Knowledge Graphs ##### The question no chunk could answer A consulting firm in Gurugram had a well-built RAG system over 2,400 client project reports. Specific questions worked beautifully — "what was the scope of the Tata Motors engagement?" returned the right paragraph with a citation. Then a partner asked: *"What are the recurring reasons our manufacturing engagements run over budget?"* The system retrieved five chunks about specific overruns and produced a summary of those five. The real answer required reading 180 reports, noticing that 60 of them mentioned overruns, and identifying the four patterns that recurred across them. **No individual chunk contains the answer to a global question, so no amount of chunk retrieval will find it.** Top-k retrieval is structurally incapable of aggregation. GraphRAG solves this by building a knowledge graph, clustering it into communities, summarising each community, and answering global questions from those summaries. The Gurugram team's answer came back with four themes, each grounded in a named set of projects. It also cost ₹87,000 to index 2,400 reports. Today is about both halves of that — what GraphRAG does that vector RAG cannot, and whether the cost is justified for your corpus. ##### Local versus global questions The distinction that determines everything: | | Local | Global | |---|---|---| | Example | "What is the notice period in the Acme MSA?" | "What contract terms do we most often negotiate?" | | Answer lives in | One or a few chunks | Patterns across many documents | | Vector RAG | **Excellent** | Fails | | GraphRAG | Good | **Excellent** | | Typical share of queries | 80–90% | 10–20% | **Most queries are local**, which is why vector RAG is the default and why GraphRAG is a supplement rather than a replacement. But the global questions are often the ones executives ask, and being unable to answer them is conspicuous. ##### Knowledge graph basics A knowledge graph stores **entities** as nodes and **relationships** as typed edges. ``` (Tata Motors)──[CLIENT_OF]──→(Manufacturing Practice) │ │ [ENGAGED_IN] [LED_BY] ↓ ↓ (Supply Chain Redesign) (Priya Sharma) │ [ENCOUNTERED] ↓ (Scope Creep)──[CAUSED_BY]──→(Unclear Requirements) ``` The power is **multi-hop traversal**. "Which partners led engagements that hit scope creep?" is two hops in a graph and effectively impossible with chunk retrieval, because no single chunk connects a partner to a failure mode via an engagement. ##### Entity and relation extraction The ingestion cost centre. An LLM reads each chunk and emits structured triples. ```python from pydantic import BaseModel, Field from typing import Literal from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI() ENTITY_TYPES = ["ORGANIZATION", "PERSON", "PROJECT", "TECHNOLOGY", "ISSUE", "OUTCOME", "LOCATION"] class Entity(BaseModel): name: str = Field(..., description="Canonical name, title case") type: Literal["ORGANIZATION", "PERSON", "PROJECT", "TECHNOLOGY", "ISSUE", "OUTCOME", "LOCATION"] description: str = Field(..., description="One sentence from this text") class Relationship(BaseModel): source: str target: str type: str = Field(..., description="UPPER_SNAKE_CASE verb phrase") description: str strength: int = Field(..., ge=1, le=10) class Extraction(BaseModel): entities: list[Entity] relationships: list[Relationship] EXTRACT_SYSTEM = f"""Extract entities and relationships from the text. Entity types: {", ".join(ENTITY_TYPES)} Rules: - Use canonical names. "Tata Motors Ltd", "TML", "Tata Motors" → "Tata Motors". - Only extract relationships explicitly stated or clearly implied in THIS text. - Relationship type must be UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, e.g. ENCOUNTERED, LED_BY, CAUSED_BY. - strength: 1-10, how central this relationship is to the text. - Both source and target must appear in the entities list. - Do not invent entities to make the graph look richer.""" def extract_graph(text: str, model="gpt-4o-mini") -> Extraction: completion = client.beta.chat.completions.parse( model=model, temperature=0.0, response_format=Extraction, messages=[{"role": "system", "content": EXTRACT_SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": text[:6000]}], ) return completion.choices[0].message.parsed ``` **Gleaning** — asking the model whether it missed anything — measurably improves recall: ```python GLEAN_PROMPT = """You extracted these entities from the text: {entities} Review the text again. List any entities or relationships you MISSED. If none, respond with empty lists.""" def extract_with_gleaning(text, max_gleanings=1, model="gpt-4o-mini"): result = extract_graph(text, model) for _ in range(max_gleanings): names = ", ".join(e.name for e in result.entities) completion = client.beta.chat.completions.parse( model=model, temperature=0.0, response_format=Extraction, messages=[ {"role": "system", "content": EXTRACT_SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": text[:6000]}, {"role": "assistant", "content": result.model_dump_json()}, {"role": "user", "content": GLEAN_PROMPT.format(entities=names)}, ], ) extra = completion.choices[0].message.parsed if not extra.entities and not extra.relationships: break result.entities.extend(extra.entities) result.relationships.extend(extra.relationships) return result ``` Microsoft's GraphRAG uses up to two gleanings by default. Each one is another LLM call per chunk, so it roughly doubles or triples ingestion cost — worth it when recall matters. ##### Entity resolution The step that determines whether your graph is useful or a mess. The same entity appears as "Tata Motors", "TML", "Tata Motors Limited", and "the client" across different chunks. ```python import numpy as np from collections import defaultdict from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer def resolve_entities(entities, embedder, similarity_threshold=0.88): """Merge duplicate entities by name similarity, within type.""" by_type = defaultdict(list) for e in entities: by_type[e.type].append(e) canonical, alias_map = [], {} for etype, group in by_type.items(): names = [e.name for e in group] emb = embedder.encode(names, normalize_embeddings=True) assigned = {} for i, e in enumerate(group): matched = None for j, c in enumerate(canonical): if c["type"] != etype: continue if float(emb[i] @ c["embedding"]) >= similarity_threshold: matched = j break if matched is not None: canonical[matched]["aliases"].add(e.name) canonical[matched]["descriptions"].append(e.description) alias_map[e.name] = canonical[matched]["name"] else: canonical.append({ "name": e.name, "type": etype, "embedding": emb[i], "aliases": {e.name}, "descriptions": [e.description], }) alias_map[e.name] = e.name return canonical, alias_map def merge_descriptions(descriptions, llm, max_input=8): """Summarise multiple descriptions of the same entity into one.""" if len(descriptions) == 1: return descriptions[0] joined = "\n- ".join(descriptions[:max_input]) return llm(f"Combine these descriptions of the same entity into one " f"comprehensive 2-sentence description:\n- {joined}") ``` **Threshold tuning matters.** 0.88 is a reasonable start; too low merges "Tata Motors" with "Tata Consultancy Services", too high leaves duplicates. **Resolve within entity type** — a PERSON should never merge with an ORGANIZATION regardless of name similarity. **Merging descriptions requires an LLM call per multi-description entity**, which is another ingestion cost. For entities appearing in 200 chunks you have 200 descriptions to reconcile. ##### Building and storing the graph ```python import networkx as nx def build_graph(extractions, alias_map, resolved_entities): G = nx.MultiDiGraph() for ent in resolved_entities: G.add_node(ent["name"], type=ent["type"], aliases=list(ent["aliases"]), description=ent.get("merged_description", ""), n_mentions=len(ent["descriptions"])) for ex in extractions: for rel in ex.relationships: src = alias_map.get(rel.source) tgt = alias_map.get(rel.target) if not src or not tgt or src == tgt: continue G.add_edge(src, tgt, type=rel.type, description=rel.description, weight=rel.strength) return G def graph_stats(G): und = G.to_undirected() degrees = dict(G.degree()) return { "nodes": G.number_of_nodes(), "edges": G.number_of_edges(), "components": nx.number_connected_components(und), "largest_component_pct": round( 100 * len(max(nx.connected_components(und), key=len)) / G.number_of_nodes(), 1), "mean_degree": round(sum(degrees.values()) / max(len(degrees), 1), 2), "top_entities": sorted(degrees.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])[:10], } ``` **`largest_component_pct` is the health metric.** A well-formed graph has 80%+ of nodes in one connected component. If you have 400 disconnected fragments, entity resolution failed and the graph cannot support traversal. **For production, use a graph database** — Neo4j, Memgraph, or Amazon Neptune — which gives you Cypher queries, persistence, and indexes: ```cypher // Which partners led engagements that hit scope creep? MATCH (p:PERSON)-[:LED_BY]-(proj:PROJECT)-[:ENCOUNTERED]->(i:ISSUE) WHERE i.name CONTAINS 'Scope Creep' RETURN p.name, collect(proj.name) AS projects, count(proj) AS n ORDER BY n DESC ``` That two-hop query is the thing vector retrieval structurally cannot do. ##### Community detection and summaries The mechanism that answers global questions. Cluster the graph into communities of densely-connected entities, then summarise each. ```python import networkx as nx def detect_communities(G, resolution=1.0, levels=3, seed=42): """Hierarchical Leiden-style clustering. Returns communities per level.""" try: from graspologic.partition import hierarchical_leiden und = nx.Graph(G.to_undirected()) clusters = hierarchical_leiden(und, max_cluster_size=12, random_seed=seed) by_level = {} for c in clusters: by_level.setdefault(c.level, {}).setdefault(c.cluster, []).append(c.node) return by_level except ImportError: # Fallback: Louvain, single level und = nx.Graph(G.to_undirected()) parts = nx.community.louvain_communities(und, resolution=resolution, seed=seed) return {0: {i: list(p) for i, p in enumerate(parts)}} COMMUNITY_SUMMARY_PROMPT = """You are summarising a community of related entities from a knowledge graph built over consulting project reports. ENTITIES: {entities} RELATIONSHIPS: {relationships} Write a report covering: 1. TITLE: a short descriptive name for this community 2. SUMMARY: what this community is about (3-4 sentences) 3. KEY FINDINGS: 3-5 specific findings, each with the entities involved Preserve specific names, numbers, and outcomes. Do not generalise them away.""" def summarize_community(G, nodes, llm, max_entities=40, max_edges=60): subgraph = G.subgraph(nodes) ranked = sorted(nodes, key=lambda n: G.degree(n), reverse=True)[:max_entities] entity_text = "\n".join( f"- {n} ({G.nodes[n].get('type')}): {G.nodes[n].get('description', '')[:200]}" for n in ranked) edges = sorted(subgraph.edges(data=True), key=lambda e: -e[2].get("weight", 1))[:max_edges] rel_text = "\n".join( f"- {u} --[{d.get('type')}]--> {v}: {d.get('description', '')[:150]}" for u, v, d in edges) return llm(COMMUNITY_SUMMARY_PROMPT.format( entities=entity_text, relationships=rel_text)) ``` ```mermaid flowchart TD A["2,400 reports"] --> B["Extract entities
+ relationships"] B --> C["Resolve duplicates"] C --> D["Build graph
~8k nodes, 24k edges"] D --> E["Leiden clustering
level 0: 340 communities"] E --> F["Level 1: 42 communities"] F --> G["Level 2: 6 communities"] E --> H["Summarise each"] F --> H G --> H H --> I[("Community reports
indexed for retrieval")] ``` **The hierarchy is what makes global search work.** A narrow global question matches a level-0 community summary; a broad one matches level 2. ##### Local and global search Two distinct query paths. ```python def local_search(G, query, entity_embeddings, embedder, llm, top_entities=8, hops=1): """Entity-anchored: find relevant entities, expand, answer.""" q = embedder.encode([query], normalize_embeddings=True)[0] names = list(entity_embeddings) sims = np.array([entity_embeddings[n] for n in names]) @ q seeds = [names[i] for i in np.argsort(-sims)[:top_entities]] neighbourhood = set(seeds) for _ in range(hops): for n in list(neighbourhood): neighbourhood.update(G.predecessors(n)) neighbourhood.update(G.successors(n)) sub = G.subgraph(neighbourhood) context = "\n".join( f"{u} --[{d.get('type')}]--> {v}: {d.get('description', '')}" for u, v, d in sub.edges(data=True)) return llm(f"Answer using only these facts:\n\n{context}\n\n" f"Question: {query}") def global_search(community_reports, query, llm, embedder, level=1, top_communities=12, batch=5): """Map-reduce over community summaries.""" reports = [r for r in community_reports if r["level"] == level] q = embedder.encode([query], normalize_embeddings=True)[0] emb = embedder.encode([r["summary"] for r in reports], normalize_embeddings=True) selected = [reports[i] for i in np.argsort(-(emb @ q))[:top_communities]] # MAP: each batch of community reports produces partial findings partials = [] for i in range(0, len(selected), batch): chunk = selected[i:i + batch] joined = "\n\n---\n\n".join(r["summary"] for r in chunk) partials.append(llm( f"From these community reports, extract findings relevant to the " f"question. Include a 0-100 relevance score for each finding.\n\n" f"Question: {query}\n\nReports:\n{joined}")) # REDUCE: synthesise the partials return llm(f"Synthesise a comprehensive answer from these partial findings. " f"Prioritise higher-scored findings and cite the entities " f"involved.\n\nQuestion: {query}\n\n" f"Findings:\n\n" + "\n\n".join(partials)) ``` **Global search is map-reduce over community summaries**, which is why it can reason across 2,400 documents. It is also why one global query can cost ₹15–40 in LLM calls. ##### Cost, honestly ```python def graphrag_index_cost(n_chunks, avg_chunk_tokens=800, gleanings=1, price_in_inr_per_1k=0.0125, price_out_inr_per_1k=0.05): """Estimate GraphRAG indexing cost.""" extraction_calls = n_chunks * (1 + gleanings) extraction_in = extraction_calls * (avg_chunk_tokens + 400) extraction_out = extraction_calls * 600 n_entities = int(n_chunks * 3.5) resolution_calls = int(n_entities * 0.3) resolution_tokens = resolution_calls * 800 n_communities = int(n_entities / 8) + int(n_entities / 40) + int(n_entities / 200) community_in = n_communities * 3000 community_out = n_communities * 700 total_in = extraction_in + resolution_tokens + community_in total_out = extraction_out + community_out cost = (total_in / 1000 * price_in_inr_per_1k + total_out / 1000 * price_out_inr_per_1k) return { "extraction_calls": extraction_calls, "community_summaries": n_communities, "total_input_tokens": int(total_in), "total_output_tokens": int(total_out), "estimated_cost_inr": round(cost), "vector_rag_cost_inr": round(n_chunks * avg_chunk_tokens / 1000 * 0.0008), } print(graphrag_index_cost(24_000)) ``` **GraphRAG indexing typically costs 50–200× vector RAG indexing.** For 2,400 reports at roughly 24,000 chunks, that is the Gurugram team's ₹87,000 against roughly ₹500 for a vector index. **Cost reduction that actually works:** use a small model for extraction (`gpt-4o-mini` is adequate; the task is structured extraction, not reasoning), skip gleaning on low-value documents, summarise only the levels you will query, and index incrementally rather than rebuilding. ##### When GraphRAG wins | Query type | Vector RAG | GraphRAG | Winner | |---|---|---|---| | "What is the notice period in the Acme MSA?" | 0.94 | 0.88 | **Vector** | | "Who led the Tata engagement?" | 0.91 | 0.93 | Tie | | "Which partners worked with clients that later churned?" | 0.31 | 0.87 | **Graph** | | "What are recurring causes of budget overrun?" | 0.22 | 0.84 | **Graph** | | "Summarise our manufacturing practice's themes" | 0.19 | 0.89 | **Graph** | | "What does clause 8.1 say?" | 0.96 | 0.71 | **Vector** | **The pattern is clear.** Vector RAG wins on specific factual lookup; GraphRAG wins on multi-hop traversal and aggregation. Neither dominates. **Hybrid is the production answer:** ```python def hybrid_graph_vector(query, vector_retriever, graph_index, llm, router): """Route by query type; combine when uncertain.""" route = router.classify(query) # "local" | "global" | "multi_hop" if route == "local": chunks = vector_retriever(query, k=5) return {"answer": llm(query, chunks), "mode": "vector"} if route == "global": return {"answer": global_search(graph_index.reports, query, llm, graph_index.embedder), "mode": "graph_global"} # multi_hop: use both chunks = vector_retriever(query, k=5) graph_ctx = local_search(graph_index.G, query, graph_index.entity_embeddings, graph_index.embedder, llm, hops=2) return {"answer": llm(query, chunks, extra_context=graph_ctx), "mode": "hybrid"} ``` **Lighter alternatives worth trying before full GraphRAG:** RAPTOR from Day 20 gives you hierarchical summaries for global questions at a fraction of the cost, and it needs no entity extraction. LightRAG and nano-graphrag are simplified implementations with substantially lower indexing cost. Try RAPTOR first — if global questions are 10% of your workload, it may be sufficient. ##### Common mistakes - **Building GraphRAG for a corpus with no global questions** — expensive and pointless. - **No entity resolution**, producing a fragmented graph with hundreds of components. - **Resolution threshold too low**, merging genuinely distinct entities. - **Resolving across entity types.** - **Not measuring `largest_component_pct`**, so graph fragmentation goes unnoticed. - **Extracting with an expensive model** when a small one suffices for structured extraction. - **Summarising every hierarchy level** when you only query one. - **Full rebuild on document updates** instead of incremental extraction. - **Global search on local questions**, costing 30× for a worse answer. - **Skipping RAPTOR**, which is often 80% of the benefit at 10% of the cost. - **Not budgeting the indexing cost** before starting. ##### Hands-on: build a small graph first Your practical task extracts entities and relations from a document set and builds a queryable knowledge graph. Start with 50–100 documents so iteration is fast. Run `graph_stats` and check `largest_component_pct` — if it is below 60%, tune your resolution threshold before proceeding. Then write three Cypher or NetworkX queries that traverse two hops, and confirm they return answers vector retrieval could not. The mini project builds a GraphRAG pipeline and compares global-question answers against vector RAG. **Write the global questions first** — genuinely aggregative ones like "what themes recur" — because on specific questions GraphRAG will lose and the comparison will mislead you. Report indexing cost alongside quality; the cost ratio is as much a finding as the accuracy difference. The assignment analyses when GraphRAG outperforms vector RAG with example query types. Build the comparison table from your own measurements, then add the decision rule: what fraction of global queries justifies the indexing cost, and what cheaper alternatives you would try first. A recommendation that says "for our workload, 8% global queries did not justify ₹87,000 — we used RAPTOR instead" is a stronger answer than an unconditional endorsement. ##### Key takeaways - **No chunk contains the answer to a global question**, which is why top-k retrieval structurally cannot aggregate across a corpus. - **Entity resolution determines whether the graph works.** Merge within type, tune the threshold, and check that 80%+ of nodes are in one connected component. - **Community detection plus hierarchical summaries** is the mechanism for global search — map-reduce over community reports, not over chunks. - **GraphRAG indexing costs 50–200× vector RAG.** Budget it explicitly, and use a small model for extraction since it is structured extraction rather than reasoning. - **Route by query type and use both.** Vector RAG wins on specific lookup, GraphRAG on traversal and aggregation — and RAPTOR is often the cheaper answer if global questions are a small share of your workload.
practical_task_reference: Extract entities and relations from a document set with an LLM and build a small knowledge graph you can query.
mini_project_reference: Build a GraphRAG pipeline over a corpus and compare its global-question answers against vector RAG.
assignment_reference: Write an analysis of when GraphRAG outperforms vector RAG, with example query types for each.
